sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: The question 'how does Go do object-oriented programming?' is in almost every Go fresher interview. Go deliberately omits classes and inheritance, replacing them with structs, methods, interfaces, and embedding. Understanding this design philosophy — and being able to explain it clearly compared to Java or Python — is what separates a candidate who has thought about Go from one who just learned the syntax.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Three substitutions that replace OOP:

- **Struct replaces class.** A Go struct is data only — no methods inside the struct body. Methods are declared separately with a receiver. Compare to Python: `class User: def greet(self)...` vs Go: `type User struct { Name string }` then `func (u User) Greet() string { ... }`.
- **Interfaces are implicit.** In Java you write `class Dog implements Animal`. In Go, if `Dog` has all the methods `Animal` requires, it satisfies the interface automatically — no declaration needed. This means you can define an interface for a type you did not write.
- **Embedding replaces inheritance.** Go has no `extends`. Instead, embed one struct inside another to promote its fields and methods. It is composition, not inheritance — and it avoids the fragile base-class problem.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **Struct definition** — `type User struct { Name string; Age int }` declares a new named type with named fields
- **Struct literal and fields** — `User{Name: "Alice", Age: 30}` (named fields, recommended) vs `User{"Alice", 30}` (positional, fragile); zero-value struct `User{}` is valid
- **Value vs pointer receivers** — `func (u User) Name() string` copies `u`; `func (u *User) SetName(n string)` can mutate `u`; rule: if any method on a type needs a pointer receiver, make all methods pointer receivers for consistency
- **Method sets** — a value of type `T` can only call value-receiver methods; a value of type `*T` can call both value-receiver and pointer-receiver methods; this matters for interface satisfaction
- **Interface definition** — `type Stringer interface { String() string }` — a set of method signatures; any type with that method satisfies the interface
- **Implicit satisfaction** — no `implements` keyword; the compiler checks at assignment time; the empty interface `interface{}` (or `any` in Go 1.18+) is satisfied by every type
- **Embedding basics** — `type Admin struct { User; Role string }` embeds User; Admin automatically has all of User's fields and methods promoted

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Pointer receiver and interface satisfaction** — if a method has a pointer receiver `func (u *User) Greet()`, then `User` (value) does NOT satisfy the interface — only `*User` does. This is the most common method-set gotcha in Go fresher interviews.
- **nil interface vs nil pointer inside interface** — `var u *User = nil; var s Stringer = u` — `s` is not nil even though `u` is nil. Calling `s.Greet()` will compile but panic at runtime. Interviewers love this because it looks safe and is not.
- **Embedding is not inheritance** — embedded types do not know they are embedded; there is no `super` call; method promotion can be shadowed by defining the same method on the outer struct.
- **The empty interface `any` holds anything but loses type information** — you need a type assertion `v, ok := x.(string)` to get the concrete value back. Always use the two-value form to avoid panics.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"Go replaces classes with structs plus methods declared with a receiver, and replaces inheritance with struct embedding for composition. Interfaces are implicit — a type satisfies an interface simply by having the required methods, with no `implements` keyword. The key practical rule is: if a method needs to mutate the receiver, use a pointer receiver, and then all methods on that type should use pointer receivers for consistency, because only `*T` satisfies interfaces that include pointer-receiver methods."*
